## Solution

**Answer:** $I(\mathbb{Z}^n) = \{0\}$, the zero ideal.

**Proof.**

We must show that any polynomial $f \in k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ that vanishes on every point of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ is identically zero. We proceed by induction on $n$.

**Base case ($n = 1$).** Let $f \in k[x]$ vanish at every integer. Since $k$ has characteristic $0$ (as $\mathbb{Z}^n \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ and the integers are distinct elements of $k$), a nonzero polynomial of degree $d$ has at most $d$ roots in $k$. But $f$ vanishes at infinitely many distinct points (all of $\mathbb{Z}$), so $f$ must be the zero polynomial.

**Inductive step.** Suppose the claim holds for $n - 1$ variables. Let $f \in k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ vanish on all of $\mathbb{Z}^n$. Write
$$f = \sum_{i=0}^{d} f_i(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\, x_n^{i},$$
where each $f_i \in k[x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}]$.

Fix any point $(a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$. The univariate polynomial
$$g(x_n) := f(a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}, x_n) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} f_i(a_1, \dots, a_{n-1})\, x_n^{i} \in k[x_n]$$
vanishes at every integer $a_n \in \mathbb{Z}$, since $(a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}, a_n) \in \mathbb{Z}^n$. By the base case, $g \equiv 0$, which means
$$f_i(a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}) = 0 \quad \text{for every } i \text{ and every } (a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{Z}^{n-1}.$$

Thus each $f_i$ vanishes on all of $\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$. By the inductive hypothesis, $f_i \equiv 0$ for every $i$, and therefore $f \equiv 0$.

**Conclusion.** The only polynomial vanishing on all of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ is the zero polynomial, so
$$I(\mathbb{Z}^n) = \{0\} = (0).$$
